profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal patent-prosecution troubleshooting meeting at an IP boutique after the USPTO issued a non-final Office Action against a patent application titled "Bearing Fault Diagnosis Method Based on EEMD and LSTM." The examiner rejected the main claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 as directed to an abstract mathematical process and under §112 for allegedly lacking adequate written description for the claimed "small-sample" training and the specific EEMD-to-LSTM workflow. The agenda is to diagnose why the draft application is not landing with the examiner, identify whether the problem is claim language, specification support, or evidence strategy, and choose a response approach before speaking with the inventors. The expected outcome is a shared plan for what to amend, what evidence to rely on, and whether to prepare a declaration.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: U.S. patent drafting and Office Action responses for software-enabled industrial systems
members.background: Elena is a former USPTO examiner who now leads prosecution strategy for AI and control-systems patents at a mid-sized IP firm; she is strong on §101 and §112 positioning and routinely manages foreign-priority cases entering the U.S.
members.private_state: She wants a response that is legally clean, avoids new-matter risk, and gets the application onto an allowance path without forcing a major inventor rewrite or creating inconsistencies with the priority filing.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says there is "support in the specification," they mean there is already enough filed text and figures to amend the claims without triggering a written-description or new-matter problem.

References to the inventor's "small-sample results" point to the results package that was attached to the original Chinese-priority materials, because only filed material is safely usable for prosecution strategy.
A §101 problem is effectively "fixed" once the claims and remarks clearly tie the model steps to vibration-signal acquisition and fault diagnosis in rotating machinery as a practical application.

If they submit a declaration, it should explain the technical operation using the existing record, not introduce later-generated comparative performance data that could complicate support and priority positions.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Signal processing, machine learning, and drafting patent responses for diagnostics algorithms
members.background: Ravi has a PhD in mechanical engineering focused on vibration analytics and previously worked on condition-monitoring systems before moving into patent prosecution; he often translates inventor experiments into technical arguments for patentability.
members.private_state: He wants the response to persuade the examiner on technical merit, showcase the application's performance under sparse data, and avoid a narrow amendment that undersells the invention's real advantage.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says there is "support in the specification," they mean the application technically teaches a skilled engineer how the EEMD-preprocessing and LSTM-training pipeline actually works well enough to rebut the examiner's concern.

References to the inventor's "small-sample results" point to the newer December spreadsheet and rig-test summary the inventors sent after filing, because those are the clearest proof of the invention's advantage.
A §101 problem is not really fixed unless the response shows a concrete technical improvement, ideally with comparative accuracy or fault-feature extraction performance versus raw-signal input.
If they use a declaration, it is normal to attach updated test data and comparative charts so the examiner can see why the claimed workflow improves bearing-fault diagnosis in practice.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the amendment needs "support in the specification."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means legally sufficient written-description basis in the filed application to add or refine claim language without new matter.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means technically sufficient explanatory detail to convince the examiner that the EEMD-LSTM workflow is actually taught and implementable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In patent practice, "support" is used constantly by both legal and technical team members, so each hears a familiar, reasonable meaning and assumes the other is using the same one.

misalignment_points.topic: Which "small-sample results" they plan to rely on
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using "the inventor's small-sample results" in the response.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the results included with the original priority-filed materials: a three-fault-class bench-test appendix already in the case record.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the later December spreadsheet and turbine-rig summary showing six fault classes and updated accuracy numbers that were emailed after filing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both result sets came from the same inventors, both are informally labeled as the "small-sample" experiments, and neither participant expects the other to be talking about a different packet of results.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as having "fixed" the §101 issue
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the response should "fix the 101 problem" by making the invention look more concrete and practical.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the issue is fixed if the claims and remarks anchor the method to sensor-acquired vibration data from rotating machinery and present the steps as a practical industrial diagnosis workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the issue is fixed only if the response demonstrates a specific technical improvement, such as better fault-identification accuracy under small-sample conditions than raw-signal LSTM.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both practical-application framing and technical-improvement framing are standard ways to talk about §101 strategy, so their surface language sounds aligned even though their thresholds for sufficiency differ.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say that, if necessary, they can submit "a declaration."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a narrow Rule 132-style inventor declaration explaining how EEMD isolates bearing-fault features and how the claimed sequence is used in machinery diagnosis, based only on material already consistent with the filed disclosure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a declaration package that includes later-generated comparative tables, class-by-class accuracy numbers, and perhaps rig photos to show the technical improvement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Saying "we can always add a declaration" feels like routine prosecution shorthand, and the details of who signs it and what exhibits are attached are often postponed until drafting.

turns.inner_thought: The examiner is basically saying these claims read like math on a black box, plus the draft overreaches on the small-sample and workflow language without enough clear filed basis. I need to steer this toward a clean amendment tied to actual vibration acquisition and bearing diagnosis in rotating machinery, using only what was already in the application and priority papers. If we can anchor the steps as a practical industrial process, the 101 issue should be manageable.
turns.utterance: So, stepping back, this Office Action is really a combined 101 and 112 problem. The examiner is not seeing the claims as adequately grounded in a real bearing-diagnosis application, and we need to figure out whether that is mainly claim wording, support in the specification, or how we're presenting the story.

turns.inner_thought: The quickest way to move this examiner is to show why the workflow matters technically, especially under small-sample conditions. The later December spreadsheet and rig summary are much stronger than the older materials; they show the accuracy lift and make the EEMD stage look essential rather than cosmetic. If we foreground the small-sample advantage and the feature extraction point, the 101 and 112 concerns both get softer.
turns.utterance: My first instinct is that the fastest path is to lean harder on the inventor's small-sample results and on the point that the preprocessing stage extracts clearer fault features before the sequence model ever sees the data. That makes the whole thing look much more concrete and practical.

turns.inner_thought: Before we say anything that narrows the claim set, I need to be sure we have literal written-description basis in the filed spec and figures for decomposition, reconstructed components, and the training sequence. I do not want to invite a new-matter fight or create tension with the Chinese priority case by drafting in concepts more crisply than they were originally disclosed.
turns.utterance: Right, but before we narrow anything, I want to confirm we have support in the specification for adding language around the ensemble decomposition, the reconstructed components, and the training sequence. If we're going to amend, I want that foundation solid.

turns.inner_thought: From a technical standpoint, the spec absolutely supports it. A skilled engineer reading the description would understand the EEMD-to-LSTM pipeline, why the decomposition helps isolate fault-related content, and how the examples fit the workflow. The examiner may be understating what is already taught. I assume Elena is just asking whether the explanation is robust enough to carry the argument.
turns.utterance: I think we're in decent shape on support in the specification. It already tells that story well enough for a skilled engineer, and the fault-feature rationale comes through pretty naturally from the examples. To me, the workflow is there.

turns.inner_thought: We can use the results that were already part of the original priority materials, but only as supporting context. I do not want to turn the response into a performance-data debate or imply we need post-filing evidence to survive 101. The safest course is to mention the inventor's small-sample results only insofar as they reinforce that this is a vibration-based machinery diagnosis method, not an abstract modeling exercise.
turns.utterance: Then I do think we should use the inventor's small-sample results in the remarks, but only to the extent they reinforce that the claimed method is applied to vibration signals from rotating machinery rather than just an abstract model in the air.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—those later numbers are the best proof we have. They show a real accuracy jump across several fault classes, which is what will make the examiner take the technical improvement seriously. If the response only says 'applied to machinery,' that feels too thin for this examiner; the data should do heavy lifting.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The inventor's small-sample results should help a lot because they show a meaningful jump across multiple fault classes, and that makes the technical improvement much harder for the examiner to brush aside.

turns.inner_thought: The clean amendment is to tie the claim to sensor-acquired bearing vibration data, recite the EEMD-based decomposition before the modeling stage, and end with a diagnosis output for rotating equipment. That should be enough to fix the 101 problem without overcommitting to narrow performance language or unsupported details. Clean, practical, industrial.
turns.utterance: What I'd like to try is amending the independent claim to recite sensor-acquired bearing vibration data, decomposition before the sequence modeling, and a diagnosis output for rotating equipment. If we keep it clean, that should fix the 101 problem.

turns.inner_thought: That amendment is fine as a base, but I don't think 101 is truly fixed unless we can also show the pipeline performs better in the small-sample setting. If the examiner keeps pressing, we should be ready with a declaration that includes updated comparative data, class-by-class results, and enough concrete material to make the improvement undeniable.
turns.utterance: That sounds right to me. And if the examiner still pushes back, we can always submit a declaration to document why the pipeline performs better under small-sample conditions.

turns.inner_thought: A declaration is fine as a fallback, but only a narrow one, and only after we see whether the claim amendment and remarks work. I want it built around the filed examples and technical operation already in the record, not around later-generated data that could muddy support, priority, or consistency. First pass should stay disciplined.
turns.utterance: Yes, a declaration is available as backup. My preference would be to first draft the remarks around the filed examples and use a declaration only if the amended claims and the practical-application framing don't get us there.

turns.inner_thought: I'll pull the December spreadsheet and rig-test summary, plus the relevant spec sections, and draft language emphasizing why the EEMD-to-LSTM flow improves diagnosis under sparse data. Elena can decide how much of the materials to use, but I assume we're aligned that the response needs to show the technical merit clearly and not just relabel the claim.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll pull the inventor's small-sample materials, mark the passages that support the workflow, and prepare some language showing why the approach materially improves bearing-fault diagnosis. Then we can decide how aggressively to build that into the response.
